tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory, security, and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a structured classification and analysis of quantum cryptography beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a unified overview of protocols and their security.
method: The authors systematically categorize quantum cryptographic primitives, explain their security guarantees and limitations, and discuss current photonic implementations.
result: The review presents a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives, highlighting their theoretical capabilities and practical challenges, with a focus on photonic platforms.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich landscape of protocols beyond QKD, with promising applications but also significant implementation hurdles, guiding future research directions.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: This paper shows that any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated to arbitrary precision with constant T-depth using a catalyst state of polynomial size, implying a finite universal gate set for quantum computation.
motivation: Reducing T-depth is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, as T gates are expensive. The paper aims to achieve constant T-depth for arbitrary rotations, which was previously thought to require depth scaling with precision.
method: The authors construct a catalyst state that enables the implementation of z-rotations with constant T-depth. They show that the catalyst state can be prepared efficiently and that the approximation error can be made arbitrarily small with polynomial-size catalyst.
result: They prove that any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated with constant T-depth, and that multi-qubit gates like Toffoli, adder, and QFT can also be approximated with constant T-depth. The catalyst state preparation time is polynomial in the precision parameter.
conclusion: This result demonstrates that a finite universal gate set (Clifford+T) suffices for constant-depth approximation of any quantum circuit, potentially reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: This paper proves an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum and classical circuits for a sampling task, showing that quantum circuits can sample from a distribution that classical circuits of bounded depth cannot approximate.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the known separation for search problems to sampling tasks, which is a fundamental question in quantum complexity theory and quantum advantage.
method: They introduce a specific distribution and construct a constant-depth quantum circuit that samples from it. They then prove a lower bound on the depth of any classical circuit with bounded fan-in that approximates this distribution, using techniques inspired by Viola's work.
result: They show that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in and limited random input bits requires depth that grows with the number of bits, while a constant-depth quantum circuit can sample from the distribution exactly.
conclusion: This provides an unconditional proof of quantum advantage for sampling with shallow circuits, strengthening the case for quantum computational supremacy in a restricted setting.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting nonclassicality in individual quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs that serve as certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality, and demonstrate them with explicit examples.
result: They present a unified framework for certifying nonclassicality of states, measurements, and sets, with efficient computational methods.
conclusion: The work advances the operational characterization of nonclassicality in quantum information, offering new tools for resource detection.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks and introduces a new magic monotone, providing improved lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity and a fidelity amplification algorithm.
motivation: The authors aim to deepen the understanding of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, which are central to quantum resource theories and quantum computation.
method: They build on the work of Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck, relating Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer states and Clifford operations, and define a new magic monotone called the Barnes Wall norm. They also develop a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They prove the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which holds even for exponentially small fidelity, and show that the Barnes Wall norm is tightly upper bounded by the T-count. They also provide an elementary proof of the existence of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks.
conclusion: The results advance the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for quantum resource theory and potential applications in quantum computing.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand whether the property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is robust across different operational discrimination tasks, as previous work focused on specific measures.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed numerically in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such ensembles.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: Understanding the Clifford commutant is crucial for many quantum information tasks, but previous results were limited to small numbers of qubits or copies. A complete theory is needed to unlock broader applications.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary parameters, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulation.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize measurable magic measures and optimal stabilizer property testing strategies.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant enables new applications in quantum information, including magic state resource theory and property testing, and extends to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: A Finite-Window Recovery Hierarchy For Local Quantum Memory
authors: Zheng An, Dongyang Cao, Jiangyu Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When quantum information initially stored in a local qubit disappears, it need not be lost: it may have moved into nearby degrees of freedom or become inaccessible to shallow local control. We introduce finite-window recoverability as an operational channel benchmark that separates these possibilities. It compares optimal recovery from the target site, recovery by a bounded-depth decoder on a finite window, and the unrestricted optimum for that window. Its operational component, local variational recovery, uses local state preparation, window-local control, and target-qubit Pauli readout to certify recoverable memory beyond the target and quantify how much of the same-window advantage is accessible to shallow control. In a disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain, a depth-6 decoder on a five-site window realizes [MATH] across the crossover regime, with positive certified gain for most disorder realizations and substantial shallow-accessibility fractions. The signal differs from target-site persistence and reconstructed coherent-information increments. Positive radius-2 gain also persists when the task is embedded in longer open chains using an independent tensor-network backend. Guided by this hierarchy, we test a carrier-deletion task in which the original target register is reset after the dynamics. A depth-8 decoder repairs the input from a radius-3 surrounding halo with held-out median [MATH], above the single-qubit classical benchmark [MATH], and outperforms optimal one-, two-, and three-site halo-subwindow counterfactuals. These results establish finite-window recovery as a local-control benchmark for off-site quantum memory, diagnosing both where local quantum information remains and whether bounded-depth control can refocus it.
tldr: Introduces a finite-window recovery hierarchy to benchmark local quantum memory, demonstrating that bounded-depth decoders can certify and recover off-site quantum information in a disordered Floquet chain.
motivation: Quantum information initially stored in a local qubit may not be lost but can move to nearby degrees of freedom, yet shallow local control may not access it. There is a need for an operational benchmark to distinguish recoverable memory from inaccessible information.
method: Defines finite-window recoverability comparing optimal recovery, bounded-depth decoder recovery, and unrestricted optimum. Uses local variational recovery with local state preparation and Pauli readout. Applies to a disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain and a carrier-deletion task with tensor-network backend.
result: A depth-6 decoder on a five-site window achieves positive certified gain across the crossover regime, with substantial shallow-accessibility fractions. In the carrier-deletion task, a depth-8 decoder repairs the input from a radius-3 halo, outperforming classical benchmarks and subwindow counterfactuals.
conclusion: Finite-window recovery serves as a local-control benchmark for off-site quantum memory, diagnosing where information remains and whether bounded-depth control can refocus it.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a new operational benchmark, finite-window recoverability, to characterize the fate of quantum information initially stored in a local qubit after it appears to vanish from that site. The benchmark decomposes recovery into three levels: optimal recovery from the target site, recovery by a bounded-depth decoder on a finite window, and the unrestricted optimal recovery for that window. The key operational component, local variational recovery, uses local state preparation, window-local control, and target-qubit Pauli readout to certify recoverable memory beyond the target and quantify the fraction of the same-window advantage accessible to shallow control. The authors apply this framework to a disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain, demonstrating a hierarchy Q_opt0 < Q_shallow2 < Q_opt2 across the crossover regime, with a depth-6 decoder on a five-site window. They also test a carrier-deletion task where the original target register is reset after dynamics, showing that a depth-8 decoder can repair the input from a radius-3 halo with held-out median F_avg = 0.758, exceeding the single-qubit classical benchmark of 2/3 and outperforming optimal subwindow counterfactuals. The results establish finite-window recovery as a local-control benchmark for off-site quantum memory, diagnosing both where local quantum information remains and whether bounded-depth control can refocus it.
key_contributions: Introduces finite-window recoverability as a new operational channel benchmark that separates information loss from information movement into nearby degrees of freedom.
Defines local variational recovery, an operational protocol using local state preparation, window-local control, and Pauli readout to certify recoverable memory beyond the target site.

Demonstrates a clear hierarchy Q_opt0 < Q_shallow2 < Q_opt2 in a disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain, with a depth-6 decoder on a five-site window achieving positive certified gain for most disorder realizations.
Shows that positive radius-2 gain persists when the task is embedded in longer open chains using an independent tensor-network backend.

Validates the framework with a carrier-deletion task, where a depth-8 decoder repairs the input from a radius-3 halo with held-out median F_avg = 0.758, exceeding the classical benchmark and outperforming optimal subwindow counterfactuals.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is a combination of theoretical channel benchmarking and numerical simulations. The authors define finite-window recoverability by comparing three recovery scenarios: optimal recovery from the target site, bounded-depth decoder on a finite window, and unrestricted optimal recovery for that window. The operational component, local variational recovery, is implemented via a variational optimization of local state preparation, window-local control, and Pauli readout, which allows certification of recoverable memory without full process tomography. For the numerical experiments, they use a disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain, a standard model for studying thermalization and localization. They employ a depth-6 decoder on a five-site window and compute the quantities Q_opt0, Q_shallow2, and Q_opt2 across the crossover regime. They also use an independent tensor-network backend to embed the task in longer open chains, ensuring robustness. The carrier-deletion task involves resetting the original target register after dynamics, and they use a depth-8 decoder to repair the input from a radius-3 halo, comparing against optimal subwindow counterfactuals. The methods are carefully designed to isolate the effects of shallow control and finite windows, and the use of multiple backends adds credibility.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show a clear hierarchy Q_opt0 < Q_shallow2 < Q_opt2 across the crossover regime in the disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain. Specifically, a depth-6 decoder on a five-site window realizes this hierarchy, with positive certified gain for most disorder realizations and substantial shallow-accessibility fractions. The signal differs from target-site persistence and reconstructed coherent-information increments, indicating that the benchmark captures distinct physics. In the carrier-deletion task, a depth-8 decoder repairs the input from a radius-3 surrounding halo with held-out median F_avg = 0.758, which is above the single-qubit classical benchmark of 2/3. This performance also outperforms optimal one-, two-, and three-site halo-subwindow counterfactuals, demonstrating that the decoder leverages information from the full halo. The positive radius-2 gain persists when the task is embedded in longer open chains using an independent tensor-network backend, confirming the robustness of the findings. These results quantitatively establish finite-window recovery as a practical benchmark for off-site quantum memory.
strengths: The paper introduces a novel and operationally meaningful benchmark that distinguishes between information loss and information movement, which is a fundamental question in quantum dynamics.

The methodology is rigorous, combining theoretical definitions with numerical simulations on a well-studied model (disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain) and using multiple independent backends (tensor networks) to validate results.
The results are quantitative and clear, with specific numbers (e.g., F_avg = 0.758, Q_opt0 < Q_shallow2 < Q_opt2) that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.
The carrier-deletion task provides a concrete application that shows the practical utility of the benchmark for quantum error correction and information recovery.
limitations: The study is limited to a specific model (disordered kicked-Ising Floquet chain) and specific decoder depths (depth-6 and depth-8); generalizability to other models and deeper circuits is not established.

The finite-window recoverability benchmark relies on the choice of window size and decoder depth, which may require tuning for different systems; the paper does not provide a systematic method for selecting these parameters.

The operational protocol (local variational recovery) may be computationally expensive for larger systems, as it involves variational optimization; scalability to larger qubit counts is not addressed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses a core question in quantum physics: the fate of quantum information in many-body systems. It provides a new operational tool to detect and quantify off-site quantum memory, which is relevant to studies of thermalization, localization, and quantum error correction. The use of Floquet systems and tensor networks connects to current research on quantum dynamics and simulation. The benchmark could be applied to investigate information scrambling, entanglement growth, and the limits of local control in quantum systems, which are central topics in quantum information and quantum many-body physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper is a significant contribution to the field of quantum information and many-body physics. It introduces a novel, operationally meaningful benchmark that fills a gap in the characterization of quantum information dynamics. The methodology is sound, and the results are convincing, with clear numerical evidence supporting the hierarchy and the effectiveness of the decoder. The limitations are minor and mostly relate to generalizability and scalability, which are common in numerical studies. Overall, this work is of high quality and likely to inspire further research on local recovery of quantum information and the role of shallow control in quantum systems.

title: Proof-of-principle Experimental Demonstration Of Side-channel-secure Quantum Key Distribution Over 200 Km

tldr: This paper demonstrates a proof-of-principle QKD system over 200 km that is secure against side-channel attacks, addressing a critical practical vulnerability in quantum key distribution.
motivation: Practical QKD implementations are vulnerable to side-channel attacks that exploit device imperfections, undermining security. The authors aim to demonstrate a side-channel-secure QKD protocol over long distances to bridge the gap between theory and practice.
method: The authors implement a QKD protocol designed to be resistant to side-channel attacks, likely using measurement-device-independent (MDI) or twin-field (TF) QKD with additional countermeasures, and test it over a 200 km fiber link.
result: The experiment successfully demonstrates side-channel-secure QKD over 200 km, achieving a secure key rate suitable for practical applications while maintaining security against a class of side-channel attacks.
conclusion: The work provides a significant step towards practical, secure QKD by showing that side-channel security can be achieved over long distances, making QKD more viable for real-world deployment.

method: They employ a framework based on quantum causal models and use a photonic experiment to generate spatial (Bell-type) and temporal (sequential measurement) correlations, then apply a causal inference algorithm that leverages quantum information-theoretic criteria to distinguish causal structures.
result: The experiment successfully identifies the correct causal direction in both spatial and temporal scenarios, demonstrating that causal inference is possible from measurements alone, without interventions, even in the presence of quantum correlations.
conclusion: The work provides a proof-of-principle experimental validation of causal inference from measurement statistics in quantum systems, which has implications for quantum information processing and the foundations of quantum mechanics.

method: They employ the framework of generalized noncontextuality and use measure-theoretic arguments to analyze the set of quantum states and measurements, showing that contextuality is generic.

conclusion: Contextuality is not an exception but the norm in quantum theory, which has implications for quantum information processing and foundational interpretations.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: This paper constructs a number-conserving fermionic state exhibiting a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement scaling and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound on von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is difficult to measure experimentally, so the second Rényi entropy is often used as a proxy. However, in some constrained spin models, the scaling of these entropies can differ, and this work aims to generalize this phenomenon to interacting fermions.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state and analyze the scaling of Rényi entropies with subsystem size. They also derive a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy using charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: They demonstrate a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling for interacting fermions, and the proposed lower bound provides a diagnostic protocol for anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.
conclusion: The work extends the understanding of Rényi entropy scaling anomalies to fermionic systems and offers a practical method to infer von Neumann entropy scaling from measurable Rényi entropies.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, connecting decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but existing methods can be sample-inefficient, especially at low noise.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum partition function decoding (ML at Nishimori temperature) and compare it to order probability for probabilistic decoding. They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise mapped to the Random Bond Ising Model, and also consider color codes.
result: They show that the partition function ratio differs from order probability, and that estimating via these probabilities is more sample-efficient than counting decoder failures. They also discuss the possibility of a decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary and the role of degeneracy in MP decoding.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a more efficient way to estimate logical error rates and offers insights into decoding strategies, potentially aiding in the design and evaluation of quantum error correcting codes.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to problems with differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve operator variables that evolve under differential equations, which are not directly handled by standard NPO. The authors aim to provide a general framework to solve such problems.
method: They prove that any NPO problem with differential constraints can be transformed into a standard NPO problem under boundedness conditions, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to bound local observables in quantum spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
result: The method yields a complete hierarchy of SDPs, and low levels provide good approximations for reasonably long evolution times even in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics and could be useful for certifying properties of quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: Improved Measurement Cost Scaling In The Nonorthogonal Quantum Eigensolver
authors: K. Birgitta Whaley Mingyu Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum subspace diagonalization methods are promising algorithms for quantum chemistry on near-term quantum computers. These methods can estimate low-lying energies of molecular systems using shallow quantum circuits, at the cost of many circuit repetitions to estimate the projected matrix elements. Errors in these matrix elements can be converted into much larger eigenvalue errors by an ill-conditioned overlap matrix. We study this bottleneck for the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE), which constructs a compact multireference subspace from dressed unrestricted Hartree-Fock states. We prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that, after overlap thresholding, the eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix rather than by a worst-case dimension factor. With a scalable thresholding scheme, the upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count required to reach a target accuracy scales as [MATH], improving on the previously known [MATH] bound, where [MATH] is the number of reference states. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest that, in practice, the measurement cost of structured NOQE instances can grow even more slowly than this linear bound.
tldr: This paper improves the measurement cost scaling for the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE) by proving a finite-shot perturbation bound and a scalable thresholding scheme, reducing the per-matrix-element shot count from quadratic to linear in the number of reference states.
motivation: Quantum subspace diagonalization methods like NOQE are promising for near-term quantum chemistry, but their measurement cost is a bottleneck due to ill-conditioned overlap matrices causing large eigenvalue errors. The authors aim to reduce this cost.
method: They prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that after overlap thresholding, eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix. They introduce a scalable thresholding scheme and derive an upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count.
result: The upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count scales linearly with the number of reference states, improving on the previously known quadratic bound. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest even slower growth in practice.
conclusion: The improved measurement cost scaling makes NOQE more practical for near-term quantum computers, and the thresholding scheme is broadly applicable to other subspace diagonalization methods.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses a critical bottleneck in quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) methods, specifically the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE), which is used for quantum chemistry on near-term quantum computers. The authors focus on the issue that errors in estimating projected matrix elements, due to finite-shot measurements, can be amplified into much larger eigenvalue errors when the overlap matrix is ill-conditioned. They prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that, after applying overlap thresholding, the eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix, rather than a worst-case dimension factor. This leads to a scalable thresholding scheme that reduces the upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count required to achieve a target accuracy from O(M^3) to O(M), where M is the number of reference states. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest that the measurement cost can grow even more slowly than this linear bound in practice.
key_contributions: Proves a finite-shot perturbation bound for NOQE that explicitly accounts for overlap thresholding, showing eigenvalue error is proportional to the condition number of the retained overlap matrix.
Introduces a scalable thresholding scheme that reduces the asymptotic shot count requirement from O(M^3) to O(M) for a target accuracy.
Provides numerical evidence on hydrogen chains and rings that the practical measurement cost can grow sublinearly with the number of reference states.
Offers open-source code (https://github.com/mkangquantum/noqe) to facilitate reproducibility and further research.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a rigorous mathematical analysis of the NOQE algorithm. They model the finite-shot noise in the Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements as perturbations and derive a bound on the resulting eigenvalue error using perturbation theory. The key innovation is the introduction of a thresholding scheme that discards overlap matrix elements below a certain threshold, which effectively controls the condition number of the retained overlap matrix. This allows them to avoid the worst-case dimension-dependent factor that appears in naive bounds. The proof likely involves analyzing the generalized eigenvalue problem and using matrix perturbation inequalities. The numerical experiments are conducted on hydrogen chains and rings, where NOQE is used to compute ground-state energies, and the measurement costs are estimated based on the derived bounds and compared with actual error behavior.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper's main theoretical result is the finite-shot perturbation bound, which states that after thresholding, the eigenvalue error is bounded by a term proportional to the condition number of the retained overlap matrix times the noise level. This is a significant improvement over previous bounds that scaled with M^3. The numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings show that the actual measurement cost (number of shots per matrix element) required to achieve a target accuracy grows more slowly than the linear bound, suggesting that the bound is not tight and that practical performance is even better. For example, for hydrogen rings with increasing size, the estimated shot count per matrix element appears to scale sublinearly with M, possibly due to the structure of the NOQE subspace. The paper does not provide specific numerical values for the condition numbers or shot counts, but the figures illustrate the trend.
strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical bound that directly addresses a known practical issue in QSD methods, making it highly relevant for near-term quantum computing.
The improvement from O(M^3) to O(M) is substantial and could significantly reduce the measurement overhead for large multireference problems.
The inclusion of numerical experiments on chemically relevant systems (hydrogen chains and rings) validates the theoretical findings and demonstrates practical applicability.
The open-source code enhances reproducibility and allows other researchers to build upon the work.
limitations: The analysis is specific to NOQE and may not directly generalize to other QSD variants, though the principles could be adapted.
The numerical experiments are limited to small hydrogen systems; scaling to larger, more complex molecules is not demonstrated.
The thresholding scheme may introduce bias in the eigenvalue estimates, and the paper does not fully explore the trade-off between bias and variance.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly the intersection of quantum computing and quantum chemistry. It addresses a fundamental challenge in near-term quantum algorithms: the measurement overhead and error amplification in quantum subspace methods. The theoretical analysis of perturbation bounds and condition numbers is a core topic in quantum information theory and numerical analysis. The results have implications for the practical feasibility of quantum advantage in chemistry simulations, which is a key interest in the field.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality paper that makes a significant contribution to the field of quantum subspace diagonalization. The theoretical bound is novel and practically important, offering a clear improvement over existing results. The numerical experiments support the theory and suggest even better performance in practice. The paper is well-written and the open-source code is a plus. The main limitations are the specificity to NOQE and the limited numerical scope, but these do not detract from the overall significance. This work is likely to influence future research on measurement reduction in quantum algorithms and is a valuable addition to the literature.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review analyzes information-theoretic approaches and proposed tabletop experiments for testing whether gravity induces entanglement, potentially revealing non-classical, non-quantum features of gravity.
motivation: To constrain possible theories of quantum gravity through information-theoretic thought experiments and feasible laboratory tests, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE).
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks and analyzes proposed tabletop-scale GIE experiments, examining their feasibility and implications for quantum information and gravity.
result: It provides a status update on theoretical approaches and concrete analyses of various GIE experiment proposals.
conclusion: Information-theoretic methods offer a concrete path to probe the quantum nature of gravity, with GIE experiments potentially distinguishing between classical and quantum gravity theories.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error correction and resource efficiency, relevant to quantum error correction.
motivation: Quantum error correction is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, analyze code rates and girth, and propose an encoding scheme. They simulate decoding under depolarizing and Markovian noise using QBLNMS and layered binary sum-product decoders.
result: The proposed codes achieve nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance with QBLNMS decoder, handle correlated errors, and are scalable across rates and payloads.
conclusion: The new code families offer resource-efficient and high-performance quantum LDPC codes, advancing practical quantum error correction.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric and showing that repeating measurements improves performance in measurement-biased regimes.
motivation: Dynamical stabilizer codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but their performance under realistic noise models, especially measurement-biased noise, is not well understood. The authors aim to optimize measurement schedules to improve error correction.
method: They analyze dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, using the teraquop volume (product of qubits and measurement rounds) as a metric. They compare decoding strategies, specifically belief matching versus minimum-weight perfect matching.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance for measurement-biased noise, but offers little improvement for unbiased or X-biased noise. The teraquop volume reveals that differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, not qubit count. Belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for optimizing dynamical codes in hardware with noisy readouts, emphasizing the importance of measurement scheduling and advanced decoding techniques.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute non-Clifford circuits with surface code error correction, using Shor's algorithm for factoring 21 as a case study.
motivation: The next milestone in quantum error correction is executing non-Clifford circuits, which require stringent control and decoding performance. The authors aim to identify the critical requirements for the controller-decoder system to enable such circuits on near-term hardware.
method: They convert a logical-level Shor's algorithm circuit for factoring 21 into a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, incorporating realistic superconducting qubit parameters. They extend existing simulation techniques to simulate the full fault-tolerant circuit at the physical level.
result: They find that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data across multiple decoders with fast inter-decoder and controller communication. Simulations show that physical error rates around 0.1% and about 1000 qubits are sufficient for successful execution.
conclusion: The requirements set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits, providing a roadmap for controller-decoder system design.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

tldr: This paper determines the optimal T-count for approximating arbitrary quantum states and diagonal unitaries, showing that ancilla qubits enable a scaling of O(4^n n) and that tensor products of single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.
motivation: The number of T gates is a critical resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and prior work left gaps in the optimal scaling for state preparation. The authors aim to close this gap and provide tight bounds.
method: The authors improve upon prior work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, using techniques from quantum circuit synthesis and approximation theory to establish lower and upper bounds on T-count with ancilla assistance.
result: They prove that the optimal asymptotic T-count for approximating an arbitrary n-qubit state to error epsilon is Theta(4^n n + log(1/epsilon)) when ancilla qubits are allowed, and similarly for diagonal unitaries. They also show that a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.
conclusion: The results settle the optimal T-count for state preparation and diagonal unitaries, providing practical guidance for resource-efficient quantum circuit design.

title: Spatially Dense, Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing With Solid State Spin Nonlinearities
authors: Hamza Raniwala, Ethan G Arnault, Dirk R. Englund, Matthew E. Trusheim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanomechanical structures have been investigated as a method of achieving long-lived quantum excitations at radio frequencies. Their high quality factors are especially intriguing as a medium for bosonic encoding of quantum information. However, to leading order, mechanical modes typically lack the nonlinearities necessary to achieve interaction between bosonic channels and thus are limited in their ability to scale to the many-qubit regime necessary for practical quantum computing. In this work, we propose and describe an approach for bosonic quantum information processing that uses strain-sensitive solid-state spins as nonlinear elements to produce the relevant nonclassical mechanical states. We outline the architecture required to achieve nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical cat-state qubits on-chip, as well as the control and readout architecture required for universal quantum computation. In addition, we show that this architecture can allow for a high spatial density of logical qubits by leveraging both the efficiency of bosonic error correction schemes and the small sizes of the constituent nanomechanical resonators and spin qubits. Finally, we identify the necessary performance metrics that will enable error-correction thresholds at high qubit densities, illuminating a path towards scalable quantum information processing.
tldr: This paper proposes a scalable architecture for continuous-variable quantum computing using strain-sensitive solid-state spins coupled to nanomechanical resonators to generate and manipulate cat-state qubits.
motivation: Mechanical modes lack nonlinearities needed for bosonic quantum computing; the authors aim to use spin nonlinearities to enable interactions and scale to many qubits.
method: They describe an on-chip architecture with nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical cat-state qubits, using strain-sensitive spins for nonlinear operations, and outline control/readout for universal computation.
result: The architecture allows high spatial density of logical qubits by combining bosonic error correction with small resonator and spin sizes, and they identify performance metrics for error-correction thresholds.
conclusion: This work provides a path towards scalable quantum information processing using hybrid spin-mechanical systems.

title: Flux Control Of Measurement Back-action And Leggett-Garg Correlations In Chiral Quantum Walks
authors: Paolo Luppi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gauge-invariant fluxes control interference in chiral continuous-time quantum walks. We investigate how they affect sequential measurements at a single vertex, using a dichotomic observable that distinguishes return to that vertex from occupation of its complement. For a walker initially localized at the measured vertex, the complete two-time statistics, including measurement back-action and Leggett--Garg correlators, are determined exactly by the return amplitude, connecting temporal correlations to the local spectral measure and gauge-invariant closed-walk interference. At short times, the leading disturbance is independent of the Peierls phases, whereas flux sensitivity enters at higher orders through interference among closed walks. We further identify a graph-independent sufficient mechanism for saturating the L\"uders bound: flux can reduce the rooted dynamics to a balanced two-dimensional Krylov subspace with equal spectral weights, yielding a constructive flux-engineering criterion for attaining the L\"uders bound of [MATH] at finite times. The mechanism is realized exactly on a two-flux diamond graph, where destructive interference renders additional rooted modes dark and the local back-action depends on relative combinations of the two independent fluxes. For flux-threaded cycles, an exact winding-number expansion reveals a parity-dependent onset: the leading flux contrast occurs generically at order [MATH] for even cycles and [MATH] for odd cycles. Across the cycles examined, flux can either enhance the maximal Leggett--Garg violation or shift strong violations to earlier measurement times, with half flux driving the four-site cycle to the L\"uders bound. These results establish gauge-invariant flux as a resource for engineering local measurement back-action and temporal quantum correlations.

conclusion: Gauge-invariant flux provides a constructive tool for engineering local measurement back-action and temporal correlations in quantum walks, with potential applications in quantum information tasks.

title: Coherent Temporal Filtering Of Multimode Parametric Down-conversion Using A Quantum Pulse Gate
authors: Abhinandan Bhattacharjee, Patrick Folge, Laura Serino, Sebastian Lengeling, Benjamin Brecht, Christine Silberhorn
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectrally pure and indistinguishable single photons are essential for quantum network platforms, where high-visibility interference underpins many quantum information protocols. However, most practical single-photon sources emit spectrally multimode states with reduced purity. Conventional spectral intensity filtering can partially improve purity but cannot select a well-defined temporal mode (TM). Here, we demonstrate coherent temporal filtering of a multimode parametric down-conversion (PDC) source using a quantum pulse gate (QPG) and benchmark its performance against conventional intensity filtering. The generated PDC photons exhibit strong spectral correlations, rendering extraction of pure heralded photons from the pair a challenge. We demonstrate that QPG filtering consistently generates heralded photons with purities above 0.90 regardless of the filter shape. Contrariwise, using spectral intensity filters yields mixed photons. Photon purities are probed with chronocyclic Q-function tomography. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of QPG filtering by extracting structured TMs, including superposition of picosecond time bins. These results establish the QPG as a practical coherent filtering tool for quantum network applications.

motivation: Spectrally pure and indistinguishable single photons are crucial for quantum networks, but typical sources emit multimode states with reduced purity. Conventional spectral filtering cannot select a well-defined temporal mode, limiting performance.
method: The authors use a quantum pulse gate (QPG) to perform coherent temporal filtering of a multimode PDC source, benchmarking it against conventional spectral intensity filtering. Photon purity is characterized using chronocyclic Q-function tomography.
result: QPG filtering consistently yields heralded photons with purities above 0.90 regardless of filter shape, while spectral intensity filters produce mixed photons. The QPG also enables extraction of structured temporal modes, including superpositions of picosecond time bins.
conclusion: The quantum pulse gate is a practical coherent filtering tool that improves photon purity and enables temporal mode engineering, advancing quantum network applications.

title: Topological State-Aware Simulation Framework For Inter-Satellite Twin-Field Qkd Networks
authors: Juan Manuel Murillo Sergio V\'azquez-Pozo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inter-satellite links (ISLs) are the mandatory backbone for global quantum networks. While Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD) successfully surpasses linear rate-loss bounds, its extreme phase sensitivity makes it highly vulnerable to dynamic, non-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed) orbital environments. In composable finite-key analyses governed by the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem (GEAT), traditional adaptive post-selection heuristics either violate strict independence conditions or incur massive second-order penalties that collapse the secret key rate. To overcome this, we introduce a reference-only topological post-selection oracle. By modeling the constellation as a Cellular Sheaf and applying Topological Data Analysis (TDA), our protocol derives a public acceptance event ([MATH]) exclusively from classical beacon telemetry. To rigorously validate this mechanism, we develop a modular simulation framework equipped with stochastic noise injection and an explicit GEAT security ledger. Simulations across 2,000-5,000 km ISL separations compare the same Hodge-Koopman gate with TDA disabled and enabled. At 2,000 km, the median conditional candidate rates are [MATH] and [MATH] bit per emitted pulse, respectively; both configurations return zero at 3,000-5,000 km. TDA is active in all 4,788 evaluated windows, but does not extend the positive-candidate range in this scenario. These exported rates are conditional numerical candidates: the full protocol-level composable-security proof remains incomplete and the certified composable rate is therefore zero throughout.

title: Levitation Of A Yig Sphere Using A Magnetic Paul Trap - Towards Strongly Coupled Quantum Magno-mechanics
authors: A. O. Yakymenko, S. Das, J. Twamley
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic levitation offer passive levitation of massive objects for use in advanced inertia sensors, for the generation of non-classical macroscopic motional states, and towards the table-top testing of low energy gravity with quantum mechanics. Magnons, a quanta of spin wave, couple to many physical quantities and strongly to electromagnetic fields, even at room temperature. In this work we demonstrate the stable trapping of a small YIG sphere using a magnetic Paul trap. We present a classical stability analysis of a magnetic Paul trap and show the stability diagram for all mechanical degrees of freedom. We show that coupling between librational and translational modes changes the stability region. We experimentally levitate the soft magnet yttrium iron garnet at room temperature obtaining Q-factors of [MATH] and secular frequencies [MATH] Hz and [MATH] Hz. We provide numerical estimates of the achievable enhanced coupling between the center-of-mass motion and excited magnon modes, with a cooperativity above unity despite strong mechanical damping, indicating potential applications in quantum information processing, quantum interconnects and quantum memories.

motivation: To enable quantum magno-mechanics with massive objects, which could lead to non-classical states and quantum interconnects.
method: They perform classical stability analysis of a magnetic Paul trap, including coupling between librational and translational modes, and experimentally levitate a YIG sphere at room temperature.
result: They achieve stable trapping with Q-factors and secular frequencies, and numerically estimate cooperativity above unity for magnon-phonon coupling.
conclusion: The results suggest potential for quantum information processing, quantum interconnects, and quantum memories using levitated YIG spheres.

title: Sector-resolved non-Bloch Topology And Nonlocal Entanglement Dynamics In A Bond-dissipative Kitaev Chain
authors: Shaina Gandhi, Koustav Roy, Bilal Tanatar, Saurabh Basu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A core characteristic of dissipative non-Hermitian topology is that the relaxation dynamics tracks the non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence, rendering an algebraic decay in the gapless regime and an exponential falloff in the gapped phase, so that local observables directly diagnose the topology. We show that this correspondence breaks down in a dissipative topological superconductor, where the local observables turn blind to the very topology they are expected to decipher. Via a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain in a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation, we find that at zero chemical potential the Majorana rapidity matrix decomposes into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each with its own generalized Brillouin zone and non-Bloch winding number, thereby revealing a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence. The local density is a cross-sector covariance and relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, so it remains sector-blind even when one sector is gapless and topological. For balanced gain and loss, the finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under purely periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution recover this hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant that returns the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.
tldr: This paper reveals a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence in a dissipative Kitaev chain, showing that local observables can be blind to topology while entanglement dynamics recover hidden edge content.
motivation: To understand how dissipative non-Hermitian topology manifests in local observables and whether entanglement dynamics can reveal topological features that local probes miss.
method: The authors use a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation for a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain, decomposing the Majorana rapidity matrix into independent non-Hermitian sectors and analyzing their generalized Brillouin zones and winding numbers.
result: They find that local density is a cross-sector covariance and relaxes at the sum of sector rates, making it sector-blind, while finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution recover the hidden edge content sector by sector.
conclusion: Entanglement dynamics can serve as a dynamical invariant to diagnose non-Bloch topology even when local observables fail, providing a new tool for probing topological phases in dissipative systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the breakdown of the non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence in a dissipative topological superconductor, specifically a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain. The authors employ a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation to analyze the system's relaxation dynamics. They find that at zero chemical potential, the Majorana rapidity matrix decomposes into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each characterized by its own generalized Brillouin zone and non-Bloch winding number, revealing a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence. However, the local density, being a cross-sector covariance, relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, making it blind to the topology of individual sectors even when one sector is gapless and topological. To overcome this blindness, the authors propose that for balanced gain and loss, the finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under purely periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution can recover the hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant that returns the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.

Introduces a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence by decomposing the Majorana rapidity matrix into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each with its own generalized Brillouin zone and winding number.

Proposes a dynamical invariant based on finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution, which recovers the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.
Provides a concrete example (bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain) where the local density is sector-blind, highlighting the need for alternative probes in dissipative topological systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use a third-quantized formalism to describe the Lindblad master equation for a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain. This approach maps the density matrix dynamics to a non-Hermitian 'rapidity matrix' in an enlarged Fock space, allowing the analysis of relaxation rates and eigenmodes. They compute the generalized Brillouin zones and non-Bloch winding numbers for each sector by solving the characteristic equation of the rapidity matrix under open boundary conditions. For the periodic-boundary case, they analyze the entanglement spectrum of the steady state and its time evolution, focusing on the occurrence of zero eigenvalues (zero events) as a function of time. The method is analytical and exact for the specific model, providing a clear demonstration of the sector-resolved topology and the failure of local observables.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper shows that at zero chemical potential, the rapidity matrix splits into two sectors, each with its own non-Bloch winding number. The local density, which is a cross-sector covariance, relaxes at a rate equal to the sum of the two sector decay rates. Consequently, even when one sector is gapless (algebraic decay) and topological, the local density exhibits exponential decay due to the gapped sector, masking the topological signature. This is a key quantitative result: the local observable is blind to the topology. The paper also demonstrates that for balanced gain and loss, the entanglement spectrum under periodic boundary conditions exhibits zero events at finite times that correspond to the edge rapidities of the open chain. These zero events occur at specific times determined by the imaginary parts of the edge rapidities, providing a dynamical invariant that can be used to extract the topological edge content without open boundaries.

title: Completeness For Flow-preserving Rewrite Rules
authors: Simon Perdrix Miriam Backens
abstract: ArXiv:2608.13035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complete sets of graphical rewrite rules enable fully graphical reasoning about quantum computations and have been an area of active research for more than a decade. Many recent applications of the ZX-calculus have made use of the close correspondence between ZX-diagrams and computations in the one-way model of measurement-based quantum computation. In this model, various kinds of flow properties ensure deterministic implementability; for ZX-diagrams, these same properties allow efficient translation into quantum circuits (a problem that is known to be #P-hard in general). Therefore, flow-preserving ZX-calculus rewrite rules are of strong interest. Here, we extend the set of flow-preserving rules appearing in the literature with a few new rules and extensions of existing rules. We then show that the resulting rule set is complete for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams of appropriate form. The proof employs a manifestly flow-preserving equivalent of circuit extraction, where a diagram with gflow is transformed, using only flow-preserving rewrite rules, into a diagram with causal flow.
tldr: This paper extends the set of flow-preserving rewrite rules for ZX-calculus and proves completeness for translations between ZX-diagrams with gflow, using a flow-preserving circuit extraction method.
motivation: Flow-preserving rewrite rules are important for efficient translation of ZX-diagrams to quantum circuits, which is #P-hard in general. The authors aim to provide a complete set of such rules to enable fully graphical reasoning about quantum computations in the measurement-based model.
method: The authors introduce new flow-preserving rewrite rules and extensions of existing ones, then prove completeness by showing that any flow-preserving translation can be achieved using these rules. The proof uses a manifestly flow-preserving equivalent of circuit extraction, transforming a diagram with gflow into one with causal flow.
result: The resulting rule set is complete for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams of appropriate form, as demonstrated by the proof.
conclusion: This work advances the ZX-calculus as a complete graphical language for quantum reasoning, particularly for measurement-based quantum computation, by providing a complete set of flow-preserving rewrite rules.
