method: The authors use a multiobjective optimization perspective to numerically construct the Pareto front in the resource space of pulse energy and control duration, and analyze the physical factors that determine the feasibility boundary.
result: They identify physical factors that set the shortest control time, linking it to the system's energy spectrum and control constraints.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into fundamental limits of quantum control, which are relevant for optimizing quantum operations and understanding thermodynamic costs.

title: Transient-energy-backflow-enhanced Ergotropy In An Open Qubit Quantum Battery Assisted By An Auxiliary Oscillator
authors: Shun-Cai Zhao
abstract:
Author(s): Shun-Cai Zhao

Decoherence and dissipation in open quantum systems generally drive quantum batteries toward passive states, thereby reducing their extractable work (ergotropy). Here, we study a driven qubit quantum battery coherently coupled to an auxiliary harmonic oscillator in the presence of dephasing and diss…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 023106] Published Thu Aug 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how an auxiliary oscillator can enhance the ergotropy of a driven qubit quantum battery in the presence of decoherence and dissipation, showing that transient energy backflow can improve work extraction.
motivation: Quantum batteries suffer from decoherence and dissipation, which reduce their extractable work (ergotropy). The authors aim to find a way to mitigate this loss and enhance battery performance.
method: They model a driven qubit quantum battery coherently coupled to an auxiliary harmonic oscillator, considering dephasing and dissipation. They analyze the dynamics of ergotropy and investigate the role of transient energy backflow from the oscillator to the battery.
result: The auxiliary oscillator can induce transient energy backflow that enhances the ergotropy of the qubit battery, partially counteracting the detrimental effects of decoherence and dissipation.
conclusion: Coupling a quantum battery to an auxiliary oscillator can be a viable strategy to improve work extraction in open quantum systems, offering a practical approach to enhance quantum battery performance.

title: Directional Charging Of Topological Quantum Energy-storage Devices Driven By The non-Hermitian Skin Effect
authors: Yanlong Chang, Xiaoli Wang, And Hongrong Li
abstract:
Author(s): Yanlong Chang, Xiaoli Wang, and Hongrong Li

The skin effect is a phenomenon characterized by the exponential localization of wave functions at a boundary in non-Hermitian topological systems, demonstrating potential applications in the field of quantum information. Here we explore its application in optimizing the performance of quantum energ…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 023712] Published Thu Aug 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes using the non-Hermitian skin effect to directionally charge quantum energy storage devices, enhancing charging efficiency.
motivation: Quantum batteries are promising but face challenges in efficient charging. The non-Hermitian skin effect offers a novel mechanism for directional energy transfer.
method: The authors theoretically model a quantum energy storage device with non-Hermitian topology, analyzing how the skin effect enables directional charging and improves performance.
result: They demonstrate that the skin effect can lead to faster and more efficient charging compared to conventional schemes.
conclusion: The work highlights the potential of non-Hermitian topological effects in quantum thermodynamics, opening new avenues for quantum battery design.

title: Noise Tolerance Via Reinforcement In The Quantum Search Problem
authors: Marjan Homayouni-Sangari And Abolfazl Ramezanpour
abstract:
Author(s): Marjan Homayouni-Sangari and Abolfazl Ramezanpour

The Grover lower bound for the unstructured search problem can be surpassed when some information about the data structure is available. Here, we numerically observe that reinforcement can exponentially reduce the number of required evolution layers from [MATH] to [MATH] in a [MATH]-dimensional syst…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022423] Published Wed Aug 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that reinforcement learning can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers needed in Grover's quantum search algorithm when partial information about the data structure is available, improving noise tolerance.
motivation: Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for unstructured search, but its performance degrades with noise. The authors aim to exploit structural information to reduce circuit depth and enhance robustness.
method: They numerically simulate a quantum search algorithm with reinforcement learning to adaptively choose evolution layers, comparing the required number of layers with and without reinforcement under noisy conditions.
result: Reinforcement reduces the number of required layers from exponential to polynomial in system size, significantly improving noise tolerance and outperforming standard Grover's algorithm in noisy settings.
conclusion: Reinforcement learning can effectively optimize quantum search circuits, making them more resilient to noise and potentially useful for near-term quantum devices.

title: $\mathit{In}$ situ Rewiring Of Two-dimensional Ion Lattice Interactions Using Metastable State Shelving
authors: Ilyoung Jung, Antonis Kyprianidis, Frank G. Schroer, Thomas W. Burkle, Jack Lyons, And Philip Richerme
abstract:
Author(s): Ilyoung Jung, Antonis Kyprianidis, Frank G. Schroer, Thomas W. Burkle, Jack Lyons, and Philip Richerme

Trapped-ion lattice geometries, which determine the interactions between trapped-ion qubits, are typically governed by the balance of Coulomb repulsion forces with the external trapping potential. Here we demonstrate how the effective ion lattice geometry and resulting qubit-qubit interactions may b…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022425] Published Wed Aug 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates in-situ rewiring of trapped-ion lattice interactions using metastable state shelving, enabling dynamic control of qubit-qubit couplings.
motivation: Trapped-ion quantum simulators typically have fixed lattice geometries, limiting their flexibility. The authors aim to dynamically control ion interactions to enable more versatile quantum simulations.
method: They use metastable state shelving to selectively alter the effective trapping potential for certain ions, thereby changing the lattice geometry and the resulting spin-spin interactions.
result: They experimentally demonstrate the ability to rewire the ion lattice in situ, modifying the interaction graph and observing the corresponding changes in qubit dynamics.
conclusion: This technique provides a new tool for dynamically reconfiguring trapped-ion quantum simulators, expanding their applicability to a wider range of quantum simulation problems.

title: Fault-tolerant Resource Comparison Of Qudit And Qubit Encodings For Diagonal Quadratic Operators
authors: Samuel Godwood, Dog̃a Murat Kürkçüog̃lu, Gabriel N. Perdue, Marina Maneyro, And Alessandro Roggero
abstract:
Author(s): Samuel Godwood, Dog̃a Murat Kürkçüog̃lu, Gabriel N. Perdue, Marina Maneyro, and Alessandro Roggero

Finite local Hilbert-space truncations arise naturally in quantum simulations of lattice field theories and motivate qudit encodings, but their fault-tolerant advantage over qubit encodings remains unclear. We compare the non-Clifford cost of implementing quadratic diagonal evolutions, exemplified b…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022427] Published Wed Aug 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper compares the fault-tolerant resource costs of qudit versus qubit encodings for implementing diagonal quadratic operators in quantum simulations, focusing on non-Clifford gate counts.
motivation: Quantum simulations of lattice field theories often use finite local Hilbert-space truncations, motivating qudit encodings, but their fault-tolerant advantage over qubit encodings is unclear.
method: The authors analyze the non-Clifford cost (e.g., T-count) for implementing diagonal quadratic evolutions in both qudit and qubit encodings, likely using resource estimation techniques.
result: The paper provides a quantitative comparison of fault-tolerant resource requirements, identifying conditions under which qudit encodings may offer advantages.
conclusion: The findings inform the choice of encoding for fault-tolerant quantum simulation, potentially favoring qudits in certain regimes.

title: Agnostic Parameter Estimation With Large Spins
authors: Huining Zhang And X. X. Yi
abstract:
Author(s): Huining Zhang and X. X. Yi

The quantum Fisher information of a quantum state with respect to a certain parameter quantifies the sensitivity of the quantum state to changes in that parameter. Maximizing the quantum Fisher information is essential for achieving the optimal estimation precision of quantum sensors. A typical quan…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022612] Published Wed Aug 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies agnostic parameter estimation with large spins, focusing on maximizing quantum Fisher information without prior knowledge of the probe state.
motivation: Quantum sensors require optimal estimation precision, which depends on maximizing quantum Fisher information. However, in practice the probe state may be unknown, so agnostic estimation is important.
method: The authors analyze the quantum Fisher information for large spin systems and propose strategies to achieve optimal estimation without knowing the initial state, likely using collective measurements or adaptive schemes.
result: They derive conditions and protocols for achieving near-optimal precision in agnostic settings, demonstrating advantages over non-agnostic approaches.
conclusion: The work provides a framework for robust quantum metrology with large spins, relevant to quantum information and sensing.

title: Robust Two-qubit Gates For Semiconductor Spin Qubits Based On Dynamical Dimensionality Reduction
authors: Qi-Pei Liu, Jian Zhou, And Zheng-Yuan Xue
abstract:
Author(s): Qi-Pei Liu, Jian Zhou, and Zheng-Yuan Xue

High-fidelity two-qubit gates leverage qubit-qubit interactions and are essential for scalable quantum computation. However, environmental noise and imperfect control of the interactions are inevitable, which degrade the quality of gate operations. Here we introduce local microwave driving in conven…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022613] Published Wed Aug 12, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a robust two-qubit gate scheme for semiconductor spin qubits using dynamical dimensionality reduction and local microwave driving to suppress noise and improve gate fidelity.
motivation: High-fidelity two-qubit gates are essential for scalable quantum computation, but environmental noise and imperfect control degrade gate quality. The authors aim to design a robust gate that is resilient to these imperfections.
method: The method introduces local microwave driving in a conventional two-qubit gate setup, combined with dynamical dimensionality reduction to effectively decouple the qubit subspace from unwanted states and noise.
result: The proposed scheme significantly enhances gate fidelity and robustness against noise and control errors, as demonstrated through numerical simulations.
conclusion: The work provides a practical approach to implementing high-fidelity two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits, which is relevant for advancing quantum computing hardware.

title: Tabletop Reversibility Of Phase-covariant Operations
authors: Fangzhen Chen And Xueyuan Hu
abstract:
Author(s): Fangzhen Chen and Xueyuan Hu

Irreversibility and time-translation symmetry are both fundamental in open quantum dynamics, and it is of great importance to study the interplay between them. In this paper, we study tabletop reversibility (TTR) for phase-covariant quantum operations and obtain sharply different conclusions for fin…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022419] Published Tue Aug 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies tabletop reversibility of phase-covariant quantum operations, revealing a sharp contrast between finite and infinite dimensions.
motivation: Irreversibility and time-translation symmetry are fundamental in open quantum dynamics, and understanding their interplay is important.
method: The authors analyze tabletop reversibility (TTR) for phase-covariant operations, deriving conditions for reversibility in finite and infinite dimensions.
result: They find that TTR holds for all phase-covariant operations in finite dimensions but fails in infinite dimensions, with specific counterexamples.
conclusion: The results highlight the role of dimension in reversibility of quantum operations, contributing to the theory of quantum information and open systems.

title: Quantum Coherence And Entanglement In Wireless Quantum Batteries
authors: Jun-Jie Jiang, Jin-Di Cao, Yu-Fei Zhang, Meng-Long Song, And Dong Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Jun-Jie Jiang, Jin-Di Cao, Yu-Fei Zhang, Meng-Long Song, and Dong Wang

We investigate the charging dynamics and thermodynamic performance of a wireless quantum battery system mediated by a common structured bosonic environment. By employing a unified resource-theoretic analysis, we elucidate the distinct roles of non-Markovian memory effects and coupling symmetry in re…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022420] Published Tue Aug 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates the charging dynamics and thermodynamic performance of wireless quantum batteries mediated by a common structured bosonic environment, using resource-theoretic analysis to reveal the roles of non-Markovian memory and coupling symmetry.
motivation: Quantum batteries are a promising application of quantum thermodynamics, and understanding how environmental memory and symmetry affect their performance is crucial for practical implementations.
method: The authors employ a unified resource-theoretic analysis to study the charging dynamics and thermodynamic performance of a wireless quantum battery system, focusing on non-Markovian memory effects and coupling symmetry.
result: The paper elucidates the distinct roles of non-Markovian memory effects and coupling symmetry in the charging process, likely showing how these factors influence energy storage and efficiency.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into optimizing quantum battery performance by leveraging environmental memory and symmetry, contributing to the field of quantum thermodynamics.

title: Giant-atom Quantum Battery
authors: Lei Qiao And P. Z. Zhao
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Qiao and P. Z. Zhao

Most studies of quantum batteries have been restricted to conventional atoms whose size is much smaller than the electromagnetic modes. Here we propose a scheme for a quantum battery based on giant atoms in a coupled-resonator waveguide. Specifically, both the charger and the battery are giant atoms…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022205] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum battery scheme using giant atoms in a coupled-resonator waveguide, exploring energy storage and charging dynamics.
motivation: Quantum batteries are a key topic in quantum thermodynamics, and most studies use conventional atoms. This work introduces giant atoms to potentially enhance performance.
method: The authors model a quantum battery where both charger and battery are giant atoms coupled to a waveguide, analyzing the charging process and energy storage.
result: The scheme demonstrates efficient charging and stable energy storage, with performance dependent on giant-atom coupling configurations.
conclusion: Giant atoms offer a promising platform for quantum batteries, potentially improving charging power and capacity.

title: Pre-distillation Of Magic States Via Composite Schemes
authors: Muhammad Erew, Moshe Goldstein, Yaron Oz, And Haim Suchowski

Magic state distillation (MSD) is a cornerstone of fault-tolerant quantum computing, enabling non-Clifford gates via state injection into stabilizer circuits. However, the substantial overhead of current MSD protocols remains a major obstacle to scalable implementations. We propose a general framewo…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 022415] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a general framework for pre-distilling magic states using composite schemes to reduce the overhead of magic state distillation.
motivation: Magic state distillation is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing but suffers from high overhead, hindering scalability.
method: The authors introduce a composite scheme that combines multiple distillation protocols or states to improve efficiency, likely through a general framework that optimizes the distillation process.
result: The framework demonstrates reduced overhead compared to standard protocols, as indicated by the publication in Physical Review A.
conclusion: The proposed composite pre-distillation approach offers a promising path to more efficient magic state distillation, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Defect In Diamond With Millisecond-scale Spin Relaxation Time At Room Temperature
authors: Sounak Mukherjee, Anran Li, Johannes Eberle, Sean Karg, Zi-Huai Zhang, Mayer M. Feldman, Yilin Chen, Mark E. Turiansky, Mengen Wang, Yogendra Limbu, Tharnier O. [Phys. Rev. B 114, 074105] Published Thu Aug 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports a new defect in diamond with millisecond-scale spin relaxation time at room temperature, potentially useful for quantum sensing and networking.
motivation: To find new solid-state spin defects with long coherence times for quantum applications, as only NV and P1 centers were previously known to have millisecond T1 at room temperature.
method: The authors characterize the WAR5 defect's spin dynamics and optical spin polarization using experimental techniques and theoretical modeling.
result: The WAR5 defect exhibits a T1 of ~1 ms at room temperature, rising to ~14 minutes at 4 K, among the longest for solid-state spin defects.
conclusion: The WAR5 defect is a promising candidate for quantum technologies, expanding the toolbox of diamond defects for sensing and networking.

Adding feedback conditioned on the measurement outcomes gives rise to another type of phase tran…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 074307] Published Thu Aug 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies measurement-induced phase transitions in monitored quantum circuits with feedback, focusing on control-driven critical fluctuations across quantum trajectories.
motivation: To understand how feedback control affects critical phenomena in monitored quantum systems, which is relevant to quantum thermodynamics and information processing.
method: The authors analyze monitored quantum circuits with feedback using numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, likely employing tensor network methods.
result: They find that feedback can drive new types of phase transitions and critical fluctuations, extending the understanding of measurement-induced transitions.
conclusion: The work highlights the role of control in quantum many-body dynamics, with implications for quantum information processing and thermodynamics.

title: Mpemba Effect In Many-body Systems Near Equilibrium
authors: P. Ben-Abdallah
abstract:
Author(s): P. Ben-Abdallah

The Mpemba effect, in which a system initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than a closer one, has been observed in a wide variety of linear and nonlinear systems. Here we develop a unified framework for the Mpemba effect in many-body systems near equilibrium based on the spectral geometr…


[Phys. Rev. B 114, 074306] Published Tue Aug 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a unified spectral geometry framework for the Mpemba effect in many-body systems near equilibrium, showing that systems farther from equilibrium can relax faster.
motivation: The Mpemba effect, where a hotter system cools faster than a colder one, has been observed in various systems but lacks a unified theoretical understanding, especially for many-body systems near equilibrium.
method: The author uses spectral geometry to analyze relaxation dynamics, deriving conditions for the Mpemba effect based on the spectral properties of the system's generator.
result: The framework predicts the occurrence of the Mpemba effect in a wide class of many-body systems and provides criteria for its observation.
conclusion: The work offers a general theoretical basis for the Mpemba effect, with implications for understanding non-equilibrium relaxation in quantum and classical systems.

title: Hybrid Quantum-classical Dynamics With Stationary Thermal States
authors: Adrián A. Budini
abstract:
Author(s): Adrián A. Budini

Quantum and classical systems can consistently be coupled via nonunitary time-irreversible mechanisms. [Phys. Rev. E 114, 024125] Published Thu Aug 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper characterizes hybrid quantum-classical dynamics that converge to thermal stationary states, linking nonunitary evolution with entropy maximization.
motivation: To understand how quantum and classical systems can be consistently coupled to reach thermal equilibrium, which is fundamental for hybrid quantum-thermodynamic frameworks.
method: The author analyzes nonunitary time-irreversible coupling mechanisms and derives conditions for the stationary state to be a thermal hybrid state that maximizes hybrid arrangement entropy.
result: The paper identifies specific classes of hybrid dynamics that yield thermal stationary states, providing a characterization of such convergence.
conclusion: The findings contribute to the theoretical foundation of hybrid quantum-classical thermodynamics, potentially guiding future studies on information-thermodynamic processes in mixed quantum-classical settings.

title: Counting Observables In Stochastic Excursions
authors: Guilherme Fiusa, Pedro E. Harunari, Abhaya S. Hegde, And Gabriel T. Landi

[Phys. Rev. E 114, L022102] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for analyzing the statistics of counting observables in stochastic excursions, with applications to quantum thermal machines and biological motors.
motivation: Understanding fluctuations of observables across stochastic trajectories is essential for various fields, including quantum thermal machines and biological motors.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework to analyze counting observables in subtrajectories (stochastic excursions) of stochastic processes.
result: The framework provides a way to compute statistics of observables in excursions, potentially revealing new fluctuation behaviors.
conclusion: The work advances the understanding of fluctuations in stochastic processes, with implications for thermodynamics and biophysics.

title: Intermodal Entanglement In A Quantum Optical Model Of High-harmonic Generation Due To The Backaction On The Driving Field
authors: Ákos Gombkötő, Peter Adam, David Theidel, And Tamás Kiss
abstract:
Author(s): Ákos Gombkötő, Peter Adam, David Theidel, and Tamás Kiss

Preparation of nonclassical light with special quantum properties is essential for quantum technologies. High-harmonic generation (HHG) is a process that not only enables the creation of attosecond pulses but also has the potential to generate light with intricate quantum properties. In a recent exp…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033154] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper theoretically studies intermodal entanglement in high-harmonic generation, showing that backaction on the driving field can produce nonclassical correlations between harmonic modes.
motivation: High-harmonic generation is a promising source of nonclassical light for quantum technologies, and understanding its quantum properties is essential for applications.
method: The authors analyze a quantum optical model of HHG, incorporating the backaction of the generated harmonics on the driving field, and compute entanglement measures between the modes.
result: They find that intermodal entanglement can be generated due to the backaction, with the degree of entanglement depending on parameters such as the driving field intensity and the number of harmonics.
conclusion: The results suggest that HHG can serve as a source of entangled light, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Propagation Of The Space-time Entanglement Of Twin Photons And Twin Beams
authors: Alessandra Gatti And Enrico Brambilla
abstract:
Author(s): Alessandra Gatti and Enrico Brambilla

We investigate how the space-time entanglement of photon pairs generated by multimode parametric down-conversion (PDC) propagates away from the source. We show that the entangled two-photon probability, tightly confined in space and time at the source, quickly broadens and decays out of a focal plan…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033165] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how the space-time entanglement of photon pairs generated by multimode parametric down-conversion propagates away from the source, showing that the entangled two-photon probability broadens and decays out of the focal plane.
motivation: Understanding the propagation of spatial and temporal entanglement is crucial for applications in quantum imaging and quantum communication, where the entangled photons must be delivered to distant locations.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the propagation of the two-photon probability distribution from a multimode parametric down-conversion source, using the formalism of space-time entanglement and considering the effects of diffraction and dispersion.
result: They find that the entangled two-photon probability, initially tightly confined at the source, quickly broadens and decays when moving away from the focal plane, indicating a degradation of the space-time entanglement.
conclusion: The propagation of space-time entanglement is non-trivial and must be accounted for in practical quantum information protocols that rely on photon pairs from PDC sources.

title: Controlling Emergent Dynamical Behavior Via Phase-engineered Strong Symmetries
authors: Marc Nairn, Beatriz Olmos, And Parvinder Solanki
abstract:
Author(s): Marc Nairn, Beatriz Olmos, and Parvinder Solanki

Symmetry constraints provide a powerful means to control the dynamics of open quantum systems. However, the set of accessible control parameters is often limited. Here, we show that a tunable phase in the collective light-matter coupling of a cavity QED system induces a phase-dependent strong symmet…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033166] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that a tunable phase in the collective light-matter coupling of a cavity QED system induces phase-dependent strong symmetries, enabling control of emergent dynamical behavior.
motivation: Symmetry constraints are powerful for controlling open quantum systems, but accessible control parameters are often limited. The authors aim to expand control by exploiting a tunable phase in the coupling.
method: They analyze a cavity QED system with a tunable phase in the collective light-matter coupling, showing that this phase gives rise to phase-dependent strong symmetries. They likely use theoretical and numerical methods to study the resulting dynamics.
result: The phase-dependent strong symmetries allow for control of emergent dynamical behavior, such as steady-state selection or suppression of certain decay channels.
conclusion: The work provides a new mechanism for controlling open quantum systems via phase engineering, with potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum thermodynamics.

title: Classical Optimization Of Reduced Density Matrix Estimations With Classical Shadows Using $N$-representability Conditions Under Shot Noise Considerations

Classical shadow tomography has become a powerful tool in learning about quantum states prepared on a quantum computer. [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033167] Published Mon Aug 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper optimizes classical shadow tomography for estimating two-particle reduced density matrices by enforcing N-representability conditions, considering shot noise.
motivation: To improve the efficiency and accuracy of estimating reduced density matrices on quantum computers, which is crucial for quantum chemistry and many-body physics simulations.
method: The authors formulate a classical optimization problem that incorporates N-representability constraints on the two-particle reduced density matrix estimated via classical shadows, and analyze the impact of shot noise.
result: They demonstrate that enforcing N-representability conditions improves the estimation accuracy and reduces the number of measurements needed, even under shot noise.
conclusion: The proposed method provides a practical enhancement for quantum state tomography in near-term quantum computing, with potential applications in quantum chemistry.

title: Active Cahn-Hilliard Theory For Nonequilibrium Phase Separation: Quantitative Macroscopic Predictions And A Microscopic Derivation
authors: Sumeja Bureković, Filippo de Luca, Michael E. Cates, And Cesare Nardini

Phase-separating active systems can display phenomenology that is impossible in equilibrium. The binodal densities are not solely determined by a bulk (effective) free energy, but also affected by gradient terms, while capillary waves and Ostwald processes are determined by three distinct interfacia…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033141] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops an active Cahn-Hilliard theory for nonequilibrium phase separation, providing quantitative macroscopic predictions and a microscopic derivation.
motivation: Active systems exhibit phase separation phenomena not captured by equilibrium theories, and a quantitative macroscopic theory is needed.
method: The authors derive a macroscopic active Cahn-Hilliard theory from microscopic dynamics, incorporating gradient terms and interfacial properties.
result: They obtain predictions for binodal densities, capillary waves, and Ostwald processes, showing three distinct interfacial tensions.
conclusion: The theory provides a quantitative framework for nonequilibrium phase separation, advancing the understanding of active matter thermodynamics.

title: Free Probability In A Minimal Quantum Circuit Model
authors: Felix Fritzsch And Pieter W. Claeys
abstract:
Author(s): Felix Fritzsch and Pieter W. Claeys

Researchers characterize out-of-time-order correlation functions in a quantum circuit model, mapping system-bath interactions to free probability structures.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031027] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses free probability to analyze out-of-time-order correlators in a minimal quantum circuit model with system-bath interactions.
motivation: Understanding the growth of quantum chaos and information scrambling in many-body systems is a key challenge. The authors aim to provide a tractable analytical framework for OTOCs in a simple circuit model.
method: They map the system-bath interactions in a quantum circuit to free probability structures, enabling the computation of OTOCs using free cumulants and R-diagrams.
result: They derive exact expressions for OTOCs and show that the free probability approach captures the universal features of scrambling, including the early-time quadratic growth and late-time saturation.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that free probability provides a powerful tool for analyzing quantum chaos in circuit models, offering insights into the information-theoretic aspects of thermalization.

title: Long-Lived Mechanically Detected Molecular Spins For Quantum Sensing
authors: Sahand Tabatabaei, Pritam Priyadarsi, Daniel Tay, Namanish Singh, Pardis Sahafi, Andrew Jordan, And Raffi Budakian

motivation: To achieve high-sensitivity quantum sensing with long coherence times, integrating molecular spins with mechanical resonators offers a promising hybrid platform.
method: The authors integrate molecular spins with a mechanical resonator and use mechanical detection to read out the spin state, achieving nanotesla sensitivity and resolving local nuclear spectra.
result: They demonstrate detection of nanotesla magnetic fields and resolve local nuclear spectra, indicating long-lived spin coherence and high sensitivity.
conclusion: The hybrid approach of molecular spins with mechanical readout provides a viable path for quantum sensing applications, with potential for further improvements.

title: Pauli Propagation: A Computational Framework For Simulating Quantum Systems

tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for simulating quantum systems using Pauli propagation, covering theory, software, and applications.
motivation: Efficient simulation of quantum systems is crucial for understanding and developing quantum technologies, and Pauli propagation offers a promising approach.
method: The authors develop a computational framework based on Pauli propagation, which tracks the evolution of Pauli operators through quantum circuits, and provide a software implementation.
result: The framework enables efficient simulation of certain quantum systems, with applications in quantum error mitigation and classical simulation of quantum circuits.
conclusion: Pauli propagation is a versatile tool for quantum simulation, with potential for broad impact in quantum information science.

title: Adaptive Estimation Of Drifting Noise In Quantum Error Correction

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:

method: The paper surveys various qudit-qubit embeddings, discusses theoretical frameworks for gate decomposition using qudits, and reviews experimental implementations.
result: It demonstrates that qudits can simplify certain quantum gates (e.g., Toffoli) and provides an overview of current experimental progress in qudit-based quantum computing.

abstract:

Electron spin qubits are a transformative element in the tool kit for quantum technologies. Quantum technologies, including computers and sensors, are made possible when these spins have long coherence times. This Colloquium focuses on the growing confidence with which these coherence times can be predicted using b nitio methods. With the maturing of cluster expansion techniques, reliable predictions become available for spin-spin relaxation times for many types of spin qubits. Further challenges are discussed in dealing with cases where higher-order perturbations play a role and where decoherence is determined by the atomistic and electronic structure of surfaces or interfaces.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021001] Published Fri Apr 04, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews computational methods, particularly cluster expansion, for predicting decoherence times of solid-state spin qubits, highlighting their growing accuracy and remaining challenges.
motivation: Long coherence times are essential for quantum technologies, and predicting them computationally can guide materials and device design. The paper aims to assess the current state and future challenges of such predictions.
method: The authors review ab initio and cluster expansion techniques for calculating spin-spin relaxation times, discussing their applicability and limitations for various spin qubit systems.
result: Cluster expansion methods now provide reliable predictions for many spin qubit types, but challenges remain for cases involving higher-order perturbations and surface/interface effects.
conclusion: Computational prediction of decoherence is becoming a reliable tool, but further development is needed to handle complex environments and improve accuracy.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive Bayesian framework for multiparameter quantum estimation, deriving bounds on measurement incompatibility and showing that it can at most double the loss relative to ideal joint measurements.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits imposed by measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation, which is crucial for practical quantum metrology.
method: The authors formulate Bayesian multiparameter estimation, derive upper bounds using the pretty good measurement, and evaluate the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. They also provide an open-source package for computing these bounds.
result: They prove that measurement incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss compared to the ideal scenario, and illustrate this with applications to phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing.
conclusion: The results offer practical benchmarks for assessing precision limits in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, showing that the ideal joint measurement assumption can be a sufficient and efficient approximation.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: This paper develops a theoretical framework for robust topological quantum state transfer in long-range interacting Rydberg arrays, showing enhanced transfer efficiency and robustness against disorder.
motivation: Quantum state transfer is crucial for quantum information processing, and topological protection can provide robustness. Long-range interactions in Rydberg arrays may improve transfer fidelity and speed compared to nearest-neighbor models.
method: The authors model one-dimensional chains with long-range couplings, deriving extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Rice-Mele models that support topological edge states. They analyze both time-independent coherent edge-state dynamics and time-dependent adiabatic modulation protocols.
result: Long-range couplings enhance energy gaps, leading to substantially improved transfer efficiency and robustness against positional disorder, outperforming nearest-neighbor models.
conclusion: Long-range interacting platforms like Rydberg arrays are promising for reliable quantum state transfer, leveraging topological protection for high-fidelity operations.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: This paper presents an optimized scheme for generating caterpillar graph states using linear optics, achieving higher efficiency than fusion-based methods.
motivation: Graph states are crucial for quantum information processing, but photonic generation via fusion gates is inefficient. The authors aim to improve the generation of caterpillar graph states, which are building blocks for larger lattice states.
method: The method uses the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, employing single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements to directly generate caterpillar graph states without fusion gates.
result: The scheme requires fewer photons and achieves a success rate several times higher than fusion-based approaches for caterpillar graph states of length n.
conclusion: The LQG picture offers a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states, potentially advancing photonic quantum information processing.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries, enabling indirect on/off switching of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires halting charging to prevent reverse flow, but direct control of the charger-battery interaction is experimentally demanding.
method: The authors apply repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit to exploit a Zeno-like mechanism, dynamically reshaping the effective Hamiltonian and switching the coupling on/off. They analyze a minimal three-body model and extend to a collective many-body architecture.
result: The protocol works beyond the ideal fast-control limit, preserves the collective charging power enhancement scaling with the number of battery units, and is feasible in an NV-13C spin platform.
conclusion: Modulator-assisted Zeno control offers a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries, addressing a key challenge in quantum thermodynamics.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight Hoare-like logic for quantum programs based on Gottesman's Heisenberg representation, enabling efficient certification of properties like qubit disposal, separability, and gate transversality.
motivation: To provide a practical, lightweight verification method for quantum programs, leveraging the efficient classical simulation of Clifford circuits to reason about a common subset of quantum programs.
method: The authors formalize a Hoare logic using Gottesman's semantics for Clifford circuits, deriving Hoare triples for Clifford operations and extending to universal quantum computing via the T-gate, Toffoli, and magic state injection circuits.
result: The logic enables certification of auxiliary qubit disposal, separability across bipartitions, transversality of gates with respect to stabilizer codes, and computation of post-measurement states. It also yields a lower bound on the number of T-gates needed for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The proposed logic offers a lightweight yet powerful tool for reasoning about quantum programs, with applications in quantum error correction and resource estimation, and can be extended to universal quantum computing.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to find schedules that minimize convergence time, with applications to solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare target states via frequent measurements, but multi-channel versions with non-commuting observables lack rigorous analysis and optimization. The authors aim to provide theoretical foundations and optimal schedules for such protocols.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and use optimal control theory to find schedules that lower-bound convergence time in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain analytical bounds and optimal dragging schedules that minimize convergence time, demonstrating the approach on k-SAT examples.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and offers guidance for designing optimal schedules for measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Resource Quantification For Programming Low-depth Quantum Circuits
authors: Entong He And Yuxiang Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2166 (2026).

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices pave the way for implementing quantum algorithms that offer quantum advantages over their classical counterparts. Due to the intrinsic noise and decoherence in the physical system, NISQ machines are naturally modeled as large-scale, low-depth quantum circuits. In practice, executing such circuits requires sending program states that encode the relevant instructions to a programmable quantum computer, typically through a cloud service. Existing programming approaches designed for generic unitary transformations are computationally inefficient in the low-depth setting, and therefore remain unsatisfactory. As such, to realize NISQ algorithms, it is crucial to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits [MATH] increases. Here, we investigate the circuit complexity and the size of quantum memory, known as the program cost, required to program low-depth brickwork circuits. We establish a tight worst-case program cost of [MATH] for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-[MATH] regime. Moreover, we analyze the trade-off between the cost of describing the layout of local gates and the cost of programming them to implement the target unitaries via the light-cone argument. Our findings suggest that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.

.
tldr: This paper studies the resource cost (program size and circuit complexity) for programming low-depth brickwork quantum circuits, establishing a tight worst-case program cost and analyzing trade-offs.
motivation: Efficiently programming NISQ devices is crucial for practical quantum advantage, but existing methods for generic unitaries are inefficient for low-depth circuits.
method: The authors analyze the circuit complexity and quantum memory size required to program low-depth brickwork circuits, using light-cone arguments to trade off layout description cost and programming cost.
result: They establish a tight worst-case program cost for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-qubit regime, and show that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
conclusion: The findings provide fundamental resource bounds for programming low-depth quantum circuits, guiding the design of efficient programming strategies for NISQ devices.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

tldr: This paper characterizes the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations (CZ-complexity) needed to prepare graph states, relating it to graph transformations and rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the resource cost of preparing graph states is important for quantum information processing, as graph states are key resources for measurement-based quantum computing and quantum error correction.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and elementary edge-complementations. They then relate CZ-complexity to rank-width and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.

conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for quantifying the complexity of graph-state preparation, with implications for optimizing quantum circuits and understanding the role of entanglement in quantum information tasks.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: This paper introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a new characterization of robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) that is necessary and sufficient for computations involving Pauli measurements, and can be computed in polynomial time.
motivation: The existing Pauli Flow condition is not necessary for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, limiting the understanding of when deterministic computations are possible. A complete characterization is needed.
method: The authors define Shadow Pauli Flow, an extension of Pauli Flow, and prove that an MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. They also provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is proven necessary and sufficient for robust determinism, and it can be computed in polynomial time, providing a complete and efficient characterization.
conclusion: This work advances the theory of MBQC by providing a full characterization of determinism for Pauli measurements, which is a fundamental aspect of quantum information processing.

title: Criticality-enhanced Quantum Sensing To A Dissipative Reservoir
authors: Xian-Kun Xin, Ze-Zhou Zhang, Qing-Shou Tan And Wei Wu
abstract: Criticality is widely regarded as a potential resource to boost the performance of quantum sensing. In existing protocols of criticality-enhanced quantum sensing, the criticality typically originates either from the probe or from the detected system itself. We here propose a scheme for sensing a dissipative reservoir based on the thermal criticality induced by the probe-reservoir interaction at finite temperature. It is revealed that the strong-coupling characteristics of the probe are able to create an additional thermal criticality, which significantly enhances the sensing performance. Our proposed scheme does not require precise dynamical control and is universal to different initial states, as it is built upon the equilibrium state generated by the natural dissipative dynamics of the probe. Expanding the scope of critical metrology, our findings pave a possible route toward high-precision quantum sensing.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum sensing scheme that exploits thermal criticality induced by probe-reservoir interaction to enhance sensing of a dissipative reservoir.
motivation: Criticality is a known resource for quantum sensing, but existing protocols rely on criticality from the probe or the system itself. This work aims to use criticality arising from the probe-reservoir interaction at finite temperature, which is a new mechanism.
method: The authors analyze a probe strongly coupled to a dissipative reservoir at finite temperature, showing that the strong coupling creates an additional thermal criticality. They use the equilibrium state of the probe to perform sensing, avoiding precise dynamical control.
result: The thermal criticality significantly enhances the sensing performance, and the scheme is universal to different initial states and does not require precise control.
conclusion: The findings expand the scope of critical metrology and provide a route toward high-precision quantum sensing of dissipative environments.

title: Pulse Engineering Of Quantum Many-Body Dynamics: Emergent Scar States, Entanglement, And Nonstabilizerness
authors: Prasant Mallik, Arkaprava Sil, Sudipto Singha Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and coherently controlling the properties of interacting quantum many-body systems is a central challenge in non-equilibrium quantum physics. While in the past decades, a wide range of many-body Hamiltonians have been introduced to study quantum chaos, atypical eigenstates, and quantum resources, systematically engineering and continuously tuning these properties within a single microscopic model remains largely unexplored. Here, we employ a pulse engineering scheme to construct an effective Hamiltonian that continuously interpolates between a chaotic Heisenberg (XXX) chain with a local impurity and the ZX Hamiltonian. Along this interpolation, we identify several families of analytically tractable atypical eigenstates embedded in the excited-state spectrum with distinct entanglement and nonstabilizerness properties. In the XXX limit, these states exhibit exact plateaus in both entanglement and stabilizer R\'enyi entropy and correspond to coherent superpositions of long-range valence-bond solid (VBS) states. As the pulse strength increases, the effective Hamiltonians exhibit a hierarchy of new set of approximate entanglement plateaus in the low-energy spectrum. Interestingly, in the fully pulse-engineered ZX limit, we uncover a distinct pair of long-range entangled stabilizer eigenstates, corresponding to rainbow scar states. We further show that pulse engineering preserves the distinct chaotic and non-chaotic regimes of the original model, while that is largely absent in the dynamical generation of entanglement and nonstabilizerness. The pulse-engineered models generate nearly identical quantum resources in both regimes, revealing a partial decoupling between quantum chaos and quantum-resource generation. Our results establish pulse engineering as a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources.
tldr: This paper uses pulse engineering to construct effective Hamiltonians that interpolate between chaotic and non-chaotic regimes, revealing atypical eigenstates with tunable entanglement and nonstabilizerness, and showing a partial decoupling between quantum chaos and quantum resource generation.
motivation: The authors aim to systematically engineer and continuously tune quantum many-body properties within a single microscopic model, which is largely unexplored.
method: They employ a pulse engineering scheme to build an effective Hamiltonian that interpolates between a chaotic Heisenberg chain with impurity and the ZX Hamiltonian, and analytically identify atypical eigenstates.
result: They find exact entanglement and stabilizer Rényi entropy plateaus in the XXX limit, approximate plateaus in intermediate regimes, and rainbow scar states in the ZX limit. Pulse engineering preserves chaotic/non-chaotic regimes but generates similar quantum resources in both.
conclusion: Pulse engineering provides a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources, partially decoupling chaos from resource generation.

title: Two-atom Dicke Model With Atom-atom Interaction
authors: Han Pu Lin Jiao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactions among emitters provide a powerful means of controlling collective light--matter phenomena, yet their role in superradiant criticality has not been thoroughly investigated. Here we construct a minimal model that can yield analytical insights --- a Dicke model with two interacting atoms coupled to a single mode cavity --- to study such interaction effects. We show that interaction changes the phase boundary, and may even completely suppress the atom-photon coupling threshold for superradiance and change the universality class of the phase transition. We further study the dissipative phase transition and quantum dynamics in the presence of dissipation channels such as photon loss and spin relaxation. Our results demonstrate important roles played by the atom-atom interaction and how it can be engineered to control atom-photon coupling.

motivation: Interactions among emitters can control collective light-matter phenomena, but their effect on superradiant criticality is not well understood.
method: The authors construct a minimal Dicke model with two interacting atoms coupled to a single cavity mode and analyze the phase boundary, universality class, and dissipative dynamics.
result: Atom-atom interaction changes the phase boundary, can suppress the coupling threshold for superradiance, and alters the universality class; dissipative phase transitions are also studied.
conclusion: Atom-atom interactions play important roles in controlling atom-photon coupling and can be engineered to manipulate superradiant phenomena.

They find that the atom-atom interaction modifies the phase boundary, and in certain regimes can completely suppress the critical coupling threshold for superradiance, leading to a superradiant phase even for arbitrarily weak atom-photon coupling. Furthermore, the interaction can change the universality class of the phase transition, from the usual mean-field behavior to a different critical exponent. The paper also extends the analysis to dissipative dynamics, considering photon loss and spin relaxation, and shows that the atom-atom interaction significantly influences the dissipative phase transition and the dynamical behavior, such as the relaxation rates and the steady-state properties. The results highlight the potential of engineering atom-atom interactions as a control knob for collective light-matter phenomena.

title: Parity Floors In Quantum Denoisers: A Closed-Form Benchmark For Fixed-Map Denoising Networks
authors: Jaeuk Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fixed quantum feature maps are increasingly inserted into diffusion denoisers, but standard image benchmarks do not reveal which structural constraint limits them. We introduce CoupledPhaseTexture, a torus-diffusion benchmark with analytic heat-kernel noising that separates parity, within-sector approximation, and sample-complexity limitations. For the depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z family we prove a containment-free parity floor: all reachable features are even functions of the encoded angles while the sine components of the Bayes denoiser are odd, so the excess risk splits exactly into an inaccessible odd part and a within-sector residual. The first term is an irreducible, noise-scale-resolved lower bound holding for every even feature class, with no containment, linearity, or closedness assumption on the feature class. The obstruction is a property of the noise-conditioned denoising target rather than static representability: the floor is re-derived at each noise scale because the target's parity content changes with noise. The measured excess is dominated by the parity proxy on two distinct priors. Higher-order Z readouts improve the even sector, but entanglement does not lower the floor and re-uploading does not reliably close it. Classical controls confirm the deficit is parity rather than quantumness: a cosine-only bank is floored similarly, while adding the sine sector matches the reference. Among tested constructions, odd readouts and a noise-coupled encoder do not match the sine-carrying classical bank. These results motivate nonclassical data access or feature classes without efficient classical surrogates; they do not establish either as sufficient for quantum advantage.

title: Thermodynamics Of Learning: A Typed Four-Component Accounting Of Memory, Fit, And Value

abstract: ArXiv:2608.12791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What a finite learning device has recorded and what will hold value for it on future tasks are not the same quantity. In the [MATH] regime, data-free updates never increase [MATH]. (II) Capitalization ledger: an exact [MATH] extraction identity and a universal ledger identity give, for (F5[MATH])-stable [MATH]-local updates under a no-discarded-record-correlation condition (f), the bound [MATH] for the capitalization efficiency [MATH], together with necessary and sufficient conditions for equality. title: Shots-to-Approximate-Solution Scaling In Neutral-Atom Quantum Optimization
authors: Jaewook Ahn Junwoo Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols exhibit genuine concentration toward low-energy solution structure remains an open question. Here, we introduce a shots-to-approximate-solution metric, STS(r), where r denotes the approximation ratio, and evaluate it using postprocessed outputs modeled by a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution governed by a single effective parameter, [MATH], that quantifies concentration toward near-optimal independent sets. To extract the genuine concentration effect in the quantum data, we apply identical postprocessing to both experimental bitstrings and randomly generated bitstrings with matched excitation density, thereby constructing an excitation-matched random baseline. Experiments on programmable Rydberg-atom arrays with system sizes up to 125 sites show that quantum annealing consistently exceeds the random baseline, demonstrating enhanced concentration toward low-energy solution structure beyond what can be attributed solely to excitation density. The results further reveal two distinct target-dependent regimes. For near-exact targets with [MATH], the required shot count grows exponentially with system size and is reduced at the same exponential level by quantum annealing within the shell-model description. By contrast, for relaxed targets, the shot cost becomes effectively constant, and the corresponding quantum enhancement diminishes, with the classical postprocessing heuristic alone reaching the target in order-unity attempts. Together, these results establish an operational method for quantifying quantum optimization performance and clarify the regimes under which quantum approaches can yield practical benefits.

motivation: The open question is whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols genuinely concentrate toward low-energy solution structures, and how to quantify this performance.
method: The authors define a shots-to-approximate-solution metric (STS(r)) and model postprocessed outputs with a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution. They compare experimental bitstrings from Rydberg arrays (up to 125 sites) against excitation-matched random baselines.

title: Encoding Circuit Satisfiability In Rydberg Atom Arrays
authors: Haotian Ji, Zhangjie Qin, Zheng An, Bowen Yan, Daoheng Niu, Kunzhe Dai, Jingkai Fang, Dongyang Cao, Jiangyu Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg atom arrays natively encode the maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem through the blockade mechanism, so the Boolean circuit satisfiability problem (Circuit-SAT) can be brought onto the platform once it is reduced to MWIS. The conventional encoding of Circuit-SAT in the Rydberg atom array proceeds through conjunctive normal form (CNF) and incurs a substantial atom overhead. We introduce CAMERA (Circuit-SAT Atom-efficient MWIS Encoding for Rydberg Arrays), a method that provides MWIS encodings of Circuit-SAT instances on the king subgraph geometry of the array. CAMERA represents each logic gate as a compact weighted gadget and assembles the gadgets with a placement and routing compiler inspired by very large scale integration (VLSI) design. On random multi-gate benchmarks, the direct encoding route lowers the atom cost relative to the CNF route by an average factor of [MATH]. To demonstrate that the encoding extends from individual weighted gadgets to multi-gate arithmetic blocks, we compile a full adder and a multiplier, verifying each against its complete truth table by exact classical ground state calculations. We further showcase solving a representative Circuit-SAT instance end-to-end, from gate level compilation through a closed-system tensor-network simulation of a hardware-compatible annealing protocol on the encoded 30-atom instance to readout of a satisfying assignment. These results establish a complete encoding and simulation workflow as a proof of principle, and a concrete route toward solving a broader family of combinatorial problems on Rydberg atom arrays.

motivation: The conventional encoding of Circuit-SAT on Rydberg atom arrays via CNF incurs substantial atom overhead, limiting scalability. The authors aim to provide a more atom-efficient encoding to enable solving larger combinatorial problems on this quantum platform.
method: CAMERA represents each logic gate as a compact weighted gadget and assembles them using a placement and routing compiler inspired by VLSI design, targeting the king subgraph geometry of the array. The encoding is verified via exact classical ground state calculations and a tensor-network simulation of an annealing protocol.

conclusion: The work establishes a complete encoding and simulation workflow as a proof of principle, offering a concrete route toward solving a broader family of combinatorial problems on Rydberg atom arrays.

title: Geometry Versus Excitation Sector In The Decoherence Of Asymmetric $N$-qubit $w$ States
authors: Sougata Bhattacharyya, Sovik Roy, Fatih Ozaydin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how network geometry and excitation sector separately control pairwise entanglement decay in asymmetric multipartite [MATH] states. To disentangle these effects, we introduce an analytically tractable [MATH]-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry and its complementary-excitation partner, yielding inequivalent vertex-base (VB) and base-base (BB) pair classes that can be compared directly with symmetric [MATH]-state references. We derive closed-form concurrence dynamics under representative one-sided noise models and find that, within either excitation sector, the VB concurrence has exactly the same noise dependence as the corresponding symmetric reference, preserving a noise-independent proportional advantage wherever both remain entangled. The amplitude-damping reordering previously identified for the three-qubit Lohmayer state is therefore a cross-sector effect rather than an intrinsic fragility of the VB geometry. In contrast, the BB pair exhibits a genuine same-sector structural fragility, with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds than the VB pair under depolarizing noise and, in the [MATH]-excitation sector, under amplitude damping. The results establish network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry as distinct ingredients governing pairwise entanglement robustness in asymmetric quantum networks.
tldr: This paper analyzes how network geometry and excitation sector independently affect pairwise entanglement decay in asymmetric N-qubit W states, revealing that certain fragilities are cross-sector effects while others are structural.
motivation: Understanding the separate roles of geometry and excitation sector in entanglement decay is crucial for designing robust quantum networks.
method: The authors introduce an analytically tractable N-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry and its complementary-excitation partner, deriving closed-form concurrence dynamics under one-sided noise models.
result: They find that within each excitation sector, vertex-base concurrence matches the symmetric reference's noise dependence, while base-base pairs exhibit genuine structural fragility with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds.
conclusion: Network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry are distinct factors governing entanglement robustness, with implications for asymmetric quantum networks.

The authors introduce an analytically tractable N-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry, along with its complementary-excitation partner, to disentangle these effects. They define two inequivalent pair classes: vertex-base (VB) and base-base (BB), and compare their concurrence dynamics under one-sided noise models (depolarizing and amplitude damping) against symmetric W-state references. The key finding is that within a given excitation sector, the VB concurrence exhibits exactly the same noise dependence as the symmetric reference, preserving a noise-independent proportional advantage wherever both remain entangled. This shows that the amplitude-damping reordering previously observed for the three-qubit Lohmayer state is a cross-sector effect, not an intrinsic fragility of the VB geometry. In contrast, the BB pair shows a genuine same-sector structural fragility, with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds under depolarizing noise and, in the (N-1)-excitation sector, under amplitude damping. The paper concludes that network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry are distinct ingredients governing entanglement robustness in asymmetric quantum networks.

title: Counterexamples To The Markovity Conjecture For The Two-Receiver Broadcast Channel
authors: Mian Huang Yanxiao Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present two counterexamples to the of Gohari, Liu and Nair (ISIT 2025), which is a structural conjecture concerning the optimizers of the dual functional associated with Marton's inner bound and, if true, would greatly simplify the evaluation of Marton's inner bound. Both counterexamples are ternary-input broadcast channels with strictly positive transition probabilities and use the same nonrectangular [MATH] auxiliary structure. In each case, we exhibit an explicit non-Markov construction whose objective value is rigorously larger than that achievable by any construction satisfying the conjectured Markov structure. Both examples are obtained with the assistance of GPT-5.6 Sol and disprove the Markovity Conjecture.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture about the structure of optimizers for Marton's inner bound in broadcast channels, providing counterexamples with ternary inputs.
motivation: The Markovity Conjecture, if true, would simplify the evaluation of Marton's inner bound for two-receiver broadcast channels. The authors aim to test this conjecture by constructing explicit counterexamples.
method: The authors construct two ternary-input broadcast channels with strictly positive transition probabilities and use a nonrectangular auxiliary structure. They rigorously compare the objective value of a non-Markov construction against any Markov construction, with assistance from GPT-5.6 Sol.
result: Both counterexamples show that the non-Markov construction achieves a strictly larger objective value than any Markov construction, disproving the conjecture.
conclusion: The Markovity Conjecture is false, indicating that the structure of optimizers for Marton's inner bound is more complex than conjectured, and further research is needed to characterize them.
